query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In a Mg‐containing lightweight high‐entropy alloy initially produced as a metastable, nonequilibrium solid solution, thermally activated diffusion drives the development of chemical short‐range order that nucleates fine, Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates. This intermetallic dispersion, by refining grain boundaries and locally modifying the composition at the oxide–metal interface, stabilizes the protective oxide film during high-temperature and corrosive exposures. In contrast, if coarser intermetallic growth ensues under prolonged or higher-temperature treatment, the integrity of the passivating layer diminishes and corrosion/oxidation resistance is lost.
generation.material_initial_state: A metastable, chemically homogeneous solid-solution state of a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Controlled heat-treatment at service-relevant temperatures designed to promote diffusion‐mediated intermetallic precipitation.
generation.conditions: Comparison of samples maintained in the as-cast state versus those subjected to controlled heat treatments (e.g., moderate thermal exposure above ~150°C) in corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing solutions).
generation.structural_mediator: Fine-scale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that form along grain boundaries and within the matrix as a result of nonequilibrium chemical short-range order evolution.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated diffusion initiates chemical short-range ordering, triggering the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. When these precipitates are finely dispersed, they act to modify the local chemical composition and grain boundary characteristics, enhancing oxide film formation and adhesion. Conversely, coarser intermetallic phases can interrupt the continuity of the protective oxide layer, leading to decreased corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Heat-treated samples that develop a fine and uniform dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates will exhibit improved or retained corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state, while samples showing coarse intermetallic growth will lose their protective properties.
generation.baseline: The as-cast metastable state, where the alloy presents a single-phase solid solution with a uniform but relatively weak passivating oxide layer.
generation.boundary: Service conditions defined by temperatures above ~150°C and exposure to corrosive environments (e.g., saline solutions) where the interplay between intermetallic precipitation kinetics and oxide film stability becomes critical.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of the intermetallic precipitation processes and the quantitative relationship between precipitate size/distribution and the resulting oxide film stability remain uncertain and may be sensitive to slight compositional variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing HEA samples: one set will be left in the as-cast metastable state, and the other will undergo a calibrated heat treatment designed to induce intermetallic precipitation. Characterize both sets using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to determine phase distribution and oxide composition. Subsequently, perform potentiodynamic polarization and immersion corrosion tests as well as high-temperature oxidation tests on both sets.
measurements: Intermetallic precipitate size and distribution via TEM
Phase identification and evolution via XRD
Corrosion current density and potential via electrochemical tests
Oxide film composition and consistency via XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a significant refinement in intermetallic precipitate size/distribution compared to as-cast samples, or if enhanced fine precipitate dispersion does not correlate with an improvement in oxide film stability and corrosion/oxidation resistance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Effects of Alloying Elements and Mechanical Alloying on Characteristics of WVTaTiCr Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are among the promising candidates for the design of structural materials in advanced nuclear energy systems. The effects of Cr, V, Ta, and Ti elements and ball milling on the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of model RHEAs were investigated. The results show that W-rich BCC1 and Ta-rich BCC2 solid solution phases were generated after a long milling duration. After high-temperature sintering, the (Cr, Ta)-rich phase associated with the Laves phase was observed in the Cr-containing model RHEAs. In addition, a high level of Ti, Ta, and V contents promoted the in situ formation of oxide particles in the alloys. Complex TiTa2O7 and Ta2VO6 oxide phases were identified by TEM, which suggests a solid-state reaction of Ti-O, Ta-O, and V-O subjected to high-energy ball milling. The oxide particles are uniformly dispersed in the BCC matrix, which can result in dispersion strengthening and the enhancement of mechanical properties.

Corrosion Behavior of MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn Alloys After Ball Milling and Subsequent Spark Plasma Sintering

Abstract: Magnesium-containing multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are promising for lightweight applications due to their low density, high specific strength, and biocompatibility. This study examines two Mg-Ti-Zn alloy compositions, equal molar MgTiZn (TZ) and Mg4TiZn (4TZ), synthesized via ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering, focusing on their microstructures and corrosion behaviors. X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy revealed the formation of intermetallic phases, including Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25 in TZ, while 4TZ exhibited a predominantly Mg-rich phase. Potentiodynamic polarization and immersion tests in 0.1 M NaCl solution showed that both alloys had good corrosion resistance, with values of 3.65 ± 0.65 µA/cm2 for TZ and 4.58 ± 1.64 µA/cm2 for 4TZ. This was attributed to the formation of a TiO2-rich surface film in the TZ, as confirmed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), which contributed to enhanced passivation and lower corrosion current density. Nonequilibrium chemical short-range order in metallic alloys

Abstract: AbstractMetallic alloys are routinely subjected to nonequilibrium processes during manufacturing, such as rapid solidification and thermomechanical processing. It has been suggested in the high-entropy alloy literature that chemical short-range order (SRO) could offer a new knob to tailor materials properties. While evidence of the effect of SRO on materials properties accumulates, the state of SRO evolution during alloy manufacturing remains obscure. Here, we employ high-fidelity atomistic simulations to track SRO evolution during the solidification and thermomechanical processing of alloys. Our investigation reveals that alloy processing can lead to nonequilibrium steady-states of SRO that are different from any equilibrium state. The mechanism behind nonequilibrium SRO formation is shown to be an inherent ordering bias present in nonequilibrium events. These results demonstrate that conventional manufacturing processes provide pathways for tuning SRO that lead to a broad nonequilibrium spectrum of SRO states beyond the equilibrium design space of alloys.Subject terms: Atomistic models, Metals and alloys This
